p: וַיְרִיצוּהוּ מִן הַבּוֹר.
— They hurried him out of the pit.
בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ אִיתָא עַל זֶה: רוֹצֶה הַשֵּׁם אֶת יְרֵאָיו כְּתִיב, וְלֹא בִּירֵאָיו.
— The holy Zohar teaches concerning this: it says “Hashem favors His fearers,” with es yereiav, rather than biyereiav, “takes pleasure in His fearers.”
כְּמַאן דְּרָעֵי בִּרְעוּתֵיהּ לְאַחֲרָא וְכוּלֵי.
— Like one who willingly seeks out another, etc.
כְּגַוְנָא דָא יוֹסֵף הֲוָה עָצִיב בַּעֲצִיבוּ דְרוּחָא בַּעֲצִיבוּ דְלִבָּא וְכוּלֵי; מַה כְּתִיב וַיְרִיצוּהוּ, אִתְפַּיְּיסוּ לֵיהּ וְכוּלֵי.
— Likewise Joseph was sad, distressed in spirit and heart, etc. What does it say? “They hurried him”—they comforted him, etc.

p: הָעִנְיָן הוּא כִּי יוֹסֵף הָיָה בְּבֵית הָאֲסוּרִים עַל יְדֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁאֵירַע לוֹ בְּהַנִּסָּיוֹן, וְהָיָה עָצֵב עַל זֶה הָעִנְיָן שֶׁסָּבַל הַמַּאֲסָר.
— Joseph was imprisoned because of what occurred during his trial, and he grieved over the matter for which he endured imprisonment.

וְהָיָה נִדְמֶה בְּעֵינָיו שֶׁהוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ תִּקְוָה לְהִתְתַּקֵּן, כַּיָּדוּעַ מִלְּשׁוֹן עֶצֶב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר נֶעֱצַב הַמֶּלֶךְ עַל בְּנוֹ, שֶׁהוּא עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ תַקָּנָה.
— It seemed to him, Heaven forbid, to be something with no hope of rectification. The term etzev, grief, denotes this, as in “The king grieved over his son”—something that cannot be repaired.

וְעַל כֵּן דָּרְשׁוּ מִזֶּה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה יא) עַל פָּסוּק וְלֹא יוֹסִיף עֶצֶב עִמָּהּ, וְכֵן (שָׁם סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה כז) עַל פָּסוּק וַיִּתְעַצֵּב אֶל לִבּוֹ, שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן אֵבֶל.

— Thus the Midrash derives from this the meaning of “and He adds no sorrow with it” (Bereishis Rabbah, beginning of chapter 11), and likewise “He grieved in His heart” (there, end of chapter 27): it is an expression of mourning.
וְכַאֲשֶׁר שָׁלַח לוֹ פַּרְעֹה וְרָאָה שֶׁיִּתְגַּדֵּל עַל יְדֵי זֶה, נַעֲשָׂה לוֹ פִּיּוּס מִן הַבּוֹר, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִתְקָן הַכֹּל.
— When Pharaoh sent for him and he saw that this would lead to his elevation, he was reconciled to the pit: everything would be rectified.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר רוֹצֶה הַשֵּׁם אֶת יְרֵאָיו, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא מְפוּיָּס עִמּוֹ בָּזֶה וְהַבּוֹר הָיָה לְטוֹבָתוֹ.
— Thus “Hashem favors His fearers”: Hashem is reconciled with him in this matter, and the pit was for his good.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vayeshev 2:1: “The holy Zohar says that the sanctity of Shabbat’s rest acts to remove sadness and agitation, as it says, ‘On the day that Hashem gives you rest from your sadness and from your agitation,’ and it expounds this of Shabbat, which is ‘the day of rest.’ Sadness means worry over something that has passed, as it says, ‘The king grieved over his son,’ and similarly in Scripture. Agitation is when a person fears and trembles over something that is yet to come upon him, as it says, ‘Peoples heard, they tremble.’ The sanctity of Shabbat, at the creation of the world, was to shine upon and rectify the six days of work that had passed, as it says, ‘God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good … God finished on the seventh day His work that He had done.’ That is, the sanctity of Shabbat appeared in order to rectify all the deeds of the six days that had passed, so that they would be very good. This is the aspect of rest ‘from your sadness’: in every Shabbat this sanctity is present, to repair the sadness over all that happened in the six workdays that have passed.”

He adds the remedy that the Midrash on “He adds no sorrow with it” points to: Shabbat, which rectifies the week that has passed and so removes that grief.

Even before the deliverance, the entire deliverance stood before their faces—the deliverance of which it is written, ‘The spirit of Jacob their father revived.’ This life stood before their faces, but before its appointed time they did not perceive it. So we hope that when the time comes to reveal the glory of His kingship over us and to have mercy on the remnant of Israel, all Israel will see that the deliverance was before our faces; it was concealed only from our side. Then the verse will be fulfilled: ‘They shall be as though I had not rejected them.’”

h: Gathering Israel and Healing Broken Hearts

p: וּלְעֵיל מִפָּסוּק זֶה נֶאֱמַר בּוֹנֵה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם הַשֵּׁם נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֵּס, שֶׁהוּא מוּסָב עַל פְּרָטֵי נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּשְׁבַּר לִבָּם בְּקִרְבָּם עַל מַעֲשִׂים כָּאֵלּוּ שֶׁנִּזְדַּמֵּן לִפְנֵיהֶם, מַה שֶּׁנִּרְאֶה לָהֶם שֶׁחָלִילָה אָבַד סִבְרָם וְתוֹחַלְתָּם מֵהַשֵּׁם, וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר:

— Earlier in the psalm it says, “Hashem builds Jerusalem; He gathers Israel’s outcasts.” This refers to individual Jewish souls whose hearts are broken over such deeds they encountered, feeling, Heaven forbid, that their hope and expectation from Hashem are lost. To them it says:
לְחַזֵּק לִבָּם, בּוֹנֵה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם הַשֵּׁם, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בּוֹנֶה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם, שֶׁהוּא כְּלָל לִבּוֹת נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְזוּכָּךְ.
— To strengthen their hearts: “Hashem builds Jerusalem.” Hashem builds Jerusalem, the collective heart of Israel’s souls, so that it becomes purified.

נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֵּס, עַל יְדֵי שֶׁיְּקַבֵּץ הַנִּדָּחִים מֵאַרְבַּע כַּנְפוֹת הָאָרֶץ, כַּיָּדוּעַ מְרֻמָּז בְּבִרְכַּת תְּקַע בְּתֵיבוֹת יַחַד מֵאַרְבַּע כַּנְפוֹת, הַשֵּׁם שֶׁהוּא רָאשֵׁי תֵבוֹת חַיִל בָּלַע וַיְקִיאֶנּוּ.

— “He gathers Israel’s outcasts”: He will gather the banished from the earth’s four corners. As is known, the words “together from the four corners” in the blessing Teka hint at the Name formed by the initials of “He swallowed wealth and will disgorge it.”

וְנֶאֱמַר הָרוֹפֵא לִשְׁבוּרֵי לֵב וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹפֵא לִשְׁבוּרֵי לֵב אֵלּוּ וּמְחַבֵּשׁ תַּחְבּוֹשֶׁת סַמִּים לְעַצְּבוֹתָם, לָעַצְבוּת שֶׁלָּהֶם שֶׁנִּדְמֶה לָהֶם שֶׁאֵין תִּקְוָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לְתַקֵּן.

— “He heals the brokenhearted,” and so forth: Hashem heals these broken hearts, applying medicinal bandages to “their wounds”—their sadness at imagining, Heaven forbid, that there is no hope of rectification.

paragraphs.text: Pri Etz Chaim, Gate of the Amidah, ch. 19: “When saying, “Gather us together from the four corners of the earth,” one should intend the Name chet–bet–vav: chet with a kamatz, bet with a segol, and vav with a sheva. Its numerical value together with its vowel points is seventy-two. It is one of the seventy-two Names and is derived from “He swallowed wealth and will disgorge it.” After saying “from the four corners of the earth,” one should recite “May it be Your will, Lord our God and God of our fathers.” Rabbi Yisrael Sarug, a disciple of the Ari of blessed memory, would say this prayer: “May it be Your will to receive every drop of seed that has issued from me in vain, outside the place of a mitzvah, whether involuntarily or willingly, through thought or deed, and also all the souls held captive within the kelipah of nogah, which the kelipot have swallowed within themselves. May the kelipah disgorge them from its belly, and may El—that is, holiness—take possession of them, through Your great Name derived from the verse, ‘He swallowed wealth and will disgorge it; El will expel it from his belly.’ And through the merit of the Name YHVH: Blessed are You, Lord, who gathers…””

p: וְעַל זֶה אָמַר מוֹנֶה מִסְפָּר לַכּוֹכָבִים, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יֵשׁ לוֹ מִסְפָּר לְכָל הַבְּרוּאִים שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ כְּנֶגְדּוֹ מַזָּל וְכוֹכָב בַּשָּׁמַיִם, וּמִכָּל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁיֵּשׁ מִסְפָּר לְכָל נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁלֹּא יֶחְסַר שׁוּם נֶפֶשׁ מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַקְּדוּשָּׁה.

— Thus it says, “He counts the number of the stars.” Hashem numbers every creature in the world that has a corresponding constellation and star in heaven. All the more does He number every Jewish soul, so that no soul will be missing from the root of holiness.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְחָשַׁב מַחֲשָׁבוֹת לְבִלְתִּי יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה חָסֵר אֲפִלּוּ נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת, וְכֵן יִהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא.
— “He devises plans so that none who are banished shall remain banished from Him.” Just as not a single soul was absent at the giving of the Torah, so it will be in the future.
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר גָּדוֹל אֲדוֹנֵינוּ וְרַב כֹּחַ, לִתְבוּנָתוֹ אֵין מִסְפָּר, וְאֵין לַעֲמוֹד עַל תְּבוּנָתוֹ בְּעִנְיָנִים כָּאֵלּוּ.
— “Great is our Master and abundant in strength; His understanding is beyond number.” One cannot fathom His understanding in such matters.

וְאַחַר זֶה נֶאֱמַר רוֹצֶה הַשֵּׁם אֶת יְרֵאָיו, שֶׁסּוֹף הַדָּבָר שֶׁיַּכְנִיס הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רָצוֹן בְּלִבָּם לְהַרְאוֹת לָהֶם שֶׁהַכֹּל יְתוּקַּן, וּכְעִנְיַן הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁל יוֹסֵף שֶׁהָיָה סִימָן לְדוֹרוֹת.

— Then it says, “Hashem favors His fearers”: ultimately Hashem will instill acceptance in their hearts, showing that everything will be rectified, like Joseph’s experience, which served as a sign for future generations.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 28:6: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: What the prophets would prophesy in every generation, they received from Mount Sinai. Thus Moses says to Israel, “Those who are here with us standing today, and those who are not here with us today.” It does not say that the latter are “standing with us today,” but simply “with us today.” These are the souls destined to be created, which had no tangible existence, so that “standing” is not said of them. Although they did not exist at that time, each received his portion. Thus it says, “The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by the hand of Malachi”—not “in the days of Malachi,” but “by the hand of Malachi,” for the prophecy had already been in his possession from Mount Sinai; until then he had not been permitted to prophesy.”

Gershon Chanoch Henich Leiner of Radzin, Sha’ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut, Entrance to the Gate of Beis Yaakov 23:11: “Even through an opening as narrow as the eye of a needle, it is enough for one who truly believes that he not be troubled by the hardships that pass over him and not complain against the ways of the Holy One, blessed be He. In this garment, as he is now in this world, it seems to him that it would have been better for him not to have been created. … All the more so one who believes in Hashem and trusts in Him, that ‘He devises plans so that none who are banished shall remain banished from Him.’ In truth it is better for him that he was created than had he not been created, everything that passes over him is for his good, and the Blessed One will comfort him for all his burdens and his pain. Even if it seems to him that there are things over which one cannot be comforted, the believer should believe this too: that He can open a clear understanding for him, so that he recognizes that he is comforted and appeased over everything, and the troubles turn into consolations.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The Radziner, of the Ishbitz–Radzin school, links the same verse, “He devises plans so that none who are banished shall remain banished,” to God’s future comforting of each person, the “appeasement” Rav Tzadok draws from the Zohar on Joseph. He addresses the very despair Rav Tzadok describes, the sense that some things cannot be repaired, and answers that God can grant a clear understanding in which even these are seen as consolation.
